summary: Specifies methods, headers and content types added to HTTP/1.1 for managing resource properties, creating and managing collections, manipulating namespaces, and locking to avoid edit collisions. It is known as WebDAV. It was replaced by RFC 4918.

eli5.summary: Normally a web page is only for reading. This adds buttons for editing, copying, moving and locking files on a web server, so two people don't overwrite each other's work.

subtitle: HTTP extensions for editing, managing, and versioning web documents from remote clients.

tldr.problem: HTTP was designed for reading documents from a server, not for collaborative authoring. Multiple people editing the same document would lose each other's changes, and there is no way to manage document metadata or organize documents into collections.
tldr.mechanism: WebDAV adds new HTTP methods (LOCK, PROPFIND, PROPPATCH, MKCOL, COPY, MOVE) and headers that let clients lock resources to prevent edit collisions, query and set metadata properties, and organize resources into collections like a file system.
tldr.outcome: Web resources can be edited remotely as if they were files on a local network drive, with metadata management and locking to prevent the lost-update problem. It was superseded by RFC 4918.

facts.label: Main HTTP methods added
facts.value: LOCK, UNLOCK, PROPFIND, PROPPATCH, MKCOL, COPY, MOVE

today: RFC 2518 was published as a Proposed Standard in February 1999 and became widely deployed in web authoring applications and file synchronization tools. It was obsoleted by RFC 4918, which clarified semantics and addressed implementation experience. WebDAV remains the basis for CalDAV (calendar sync) and CardDAV (contact sync) and is still used in cloud storage and collaboration systems.

sections.title: The Problem with HTTP for Authoring
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 is an excellent protocol for retrieving documents, but it was not designed for collaborative authoring. When multiple people edit the same document through HTTP, the last person to save wins and earlier edits are lost—the 'lost update' problem.

HTTP also lacks a way to attach metadata to resources (creation date, author, document title, etc.) beyond the limited set available in HTTP headers. A collaborative authoring system needs to store and retrieve arbitrary properties.

Additionally, HTTP has no way to create or manage hierarchies of resources. A file system has directories; a web server just has a flat namespace (or simulated hierarchy through URI paths). WebDAV adds the concept of collections—resources that contain other resources—so that web content can be organized like files and folders.

WebDAV also allows copying and moving resources with a single operation, managing resource links, and most importantly, locking resources so that while one author is editing, others are prevented from making conflicting changes.
sections.eli5: Imagine trying to work on a shared document where there is no way to tell someone 'I am editing this, do not touch it.' When two people save, the last one overwrites the first. WebDAV fixes that.

sections.title: Properties, Collections, and Resources
sections.content:
WebDAV introduces three core concepts. A resource is any item in the HTTP namespace (a document, an image, a file). Every resource can now have properties—metadata name-value pairs that describe the resource. Properties include built-in ones like creation date, content type, and content length, and custom ones defined by the application (author, status, department, etc.).

Properties fall into two categories: live properties are maintained by the server (e.g., getcontentlength is computed from the entity body), and dead properties are stored verbatim as the client provides them. The server does not enforce the syntax or meaning of dead properties.

A collection is a special resource that contains a list of member resources. A collection is like a file system directory. Collections have hierarchical member URIs, so the web namespace can be organized as a tree rather than a flat list. Resources can be moved or copied with new methods, maintaining their properties.

WebDAV also introduces null resources—URIs that do not currently map to a resource but can be locked or written to. This allows clients to lock a name before creating a document, preventing race conditions.
sections.eli5: Resources are files, properties are notes about them (who wrote it, when), collections are folders, and locks prevent two people from editing the same file at once.

sections.title: Locking to Prevent Edit Collisions
sections.content:
WebDAV's locking mechanism is its answer to the lost-update problem. A client can place a write lock on a resource, making it exclusive (only one principal can hold it) or shared (multiple principals can coordinate). The lock has a token and a timeout.

While a resource is locked, any client that wishes to modify it (via PUT, DELETE, MOVE, etc.) must include the lock token in the If header. If the token is absent or invalid, the request fails with a 423 (Locked) status.

Locks are depth-aware. A lock on a collection with Depth: infinity locks the collection and all its current and future members. Locks are timeout-aware—a lock expires after a specified duration unless the client refreshes it by resubmitting the lock request without a body.

This design ensures that two clients cannot accidentally overwrite each other's changes. If Alice locks a document and begins editing, Bob will see the lock and either wait or edit a different document. When Alice's edits are complete, she unlocks the document and Bob can proceed.
sections.eli5: A lock is like raising your hand to say 'I am working on this.' Once you have the lock, others cannot change the file. When you unlock it, someone else can lock it and edit.

sections.title: Core Methods and Operations
sections.content:
PROPFIND retrieves the properties of a resource and its members (if it is a collection). It can request all properties, specific named properties, or just property names. The response is a Multi-Status (207) document listing each resource and its properties.

PROPPATCH modifies properties, allowing clients to set or remove dead properties and (in some cases) live properties. The request body contains XML with set and remove directives.

MKCOL creates a new collection (directory) at a given URI. Existing HTTP PUT is used to create or replace individual resources.

COPY duplicates a resource or collection to a new location. The Overwrite header controls whether the destination can be replaced if it already exists.

MOVE relocates a resource or collection, renaming it or moving it to a different part of the namespace. MOVE is atomic: the source is removed and the destination is created.

DELETE removes a resource or collection. Deleting a collection typically deletes all its members (implementation-dependent).

LOCK creates a lock on a resource. The request body specifies exclusive or shared scope, write-type lock, and a timeout duration. The response includes the lock token.

UNLOCK removes a lock using its token.
sections.eli5: The new methods let you look at file info (PROPFIND), set notes about files (PROPPATCH), make folders (MKCOL), copy files (COPY), move files (MOVE), delete files (DELETE), and lock them while editing (LOCK and UNLOCK).

sections.title: Compliance and Real-World Use
sections.content:
WebDAV defines two compliance classes. Class 1 servers MUST support the PUT and DELETE methods and the Depth header; they MUST support PROPFIND to retrieve property names and values. Class 2 servers additionally MUST support LOCK and UNLOCK, locking discovery, and the lock-related status codes (423 Locked, 424 Failed Dependency).

Some WebDAV methods operate on multiple resources (e.g., PROPFIND on a collection with Depth: infinity, or COPY of a collection). To report status for each resource, WebDAV introduced the 207 Multi-Status response code. A 207 response contains an XML body with a response element for each resource, each with its own status code.

WebDAV uses XML extensively for request and response bodies, chosen for its flexibility and internationalization support. XML elements are defined in the DAV namespace, and custom elements can be added via XML namespace extension.

In practice, WebDAV enabled file editing tools like Dreamweaver, Office, and Finder (macOS) to treat web resources as if they were on a network file system. A user could map a WebDAV server as a drive and edit documents with their favorite application without learning web-specific tools. WebDAV also forms the basis for CalDAV (calendar) and CardDAV (contacts) protocols.
sections.eli5: WebDAV has two levels of support: basic (read and write files) and full (locking). Real tools like Microsoft Office and Mac Finder use WebDAV to let you edit web files as if they were on your hard drive.
